## Lecture Plan

- **The Gauss-Markov Assumptions.** What has to be true of the population for any of this to work.
- **Unbiasedness.** In what sense least squares gets the right answer, and in what sense it does not.
- **Precision.** How much an estimate would move if we drew again, and why no other line does better.

# The Gauss-Markov Assumptions

## Five Claims About the Population

**The goal of this section:** state what has to be true of the population
before any of last week's arithmetic tells us anything about the world.

1. Earnings really are a straight line in schooling, plus an error.
2. The error has mean zero at every level of schooling.
3. We drew our sample at random.
4. Schooling actually varies in the sample.
5. The error has the same variance at every level of schooling.

::: {.tablenotes}
Read them as promises rather than as a checklist. Each one is doing a specific
job, and we will see which job in the next two sections.
:::

<!-- IDEA 1. 10-35 min. -->

## Which Assumption Buys Unbiasedness and Which Buys Precision

- **Two** is the one that buys unbiasedness. It is also the one that is almost
  never true outside a simulation, and weeks 8 and 12 are about that.
- **Four and five** buy precision, and a usable standard error.
- **One** is about shape, and you saw last week what its failure looks like.
- **Three** is about how the data arrived, and it is the one nobody checks.

::: {.caveat}
Assumption two is not a technicality. It says that people with more schooling
do not differ from people with less in any way that also affects earnings.
Say that out loud about this population and see whether you believe it.
:::

# Unbiasedness

## One Sample Fitted Against the Known True Line

**The goal of this section:** say in what sense least squares gets the right
answer, and then be precise about what that does not mean.

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/figures/2-3_onesample.png}{Grey is the population of 200,000.
Colour is the 120 we drew. Green is the true line; dashed navy is what our
sample says.}
```

<!-- IDEA 2. 38-63 min. -->

## Repeated Samples From the Same Population

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/figures/2-3_sampling.png}{Five hundred samples of 120 from the
same population, one slope kept from each. Green is the truth; dashed navy is
the single sample we happened to draw.}
```

::: {.result}
The histogram is centred on the truth. That is what unbiasedness means, and it
is a statement about the histogram rather than about any bar in it.
:::

## Unbiasedness Does Not Mean Your Estimate Is Right

::: {.caveat title="Read this one carefully"}
Our sample gave 1.52 when the truth is 1.30. Least squares is unbiased and our
estimate is still wrong. Those two facts are entirely compatible, and if you
leave today believing that unbiasedness means your number is right, the rest
of the module will not work.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
In real work you get one draw. You never see the histogram. Everything from
next week onwards is about what can honestly be said from a single draw.
:::

## Vote: Is This Estimator Biased?

I always drop the highest earner before fitting.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue, vote again. Then: which of the five assumptions did that break?
:::

<!-- ConcepTest 2. It breaks the random sample and it breaks zero conditional
     mean, and it is a rule most people find reasonable. Do not adjudicate. -->

# Precision

## Three Ways to Narrow the Distribution

**The goal of this section:** say how far an estimate would move if we drew
again, and what we could do about it.

```{=latex}
\figpair{../_shared/figures/2-3_precision-n.png}{Four times the
sample.}{../_shared/figures/2-3_precision-spread.png}{More spread in
schooling.}
```

<!-- IDEA 3. 66-92 min. -->

## Three Ingredients in the Standard Error of the Slope

The spread of that histogram has a name and a formula, and the formula has
exactly the three ingredients the figure has:

- more people, and it narrows
- more spread in schooling, and it narrows
- a quieter error, and it narrows

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/figures/2-3_precision-noise.png}{The third ingredient: a
smaller error variance.}
```

::: {.tablenotes}
Only the first is usually in your control. The second is a fact about who you
sampled; the third is a fact about the world.
:::

## Comparing Two Unbiased Estimators by Their Variance

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/figures/2-3_blue.png}{Least squares against an estimator that
uses only the two extreme observations. Both centre on the truth.}
```

::: {.result title="The Gauss-Markov theorem"}
Among all estimators that are linear in the data and unbiased, least squares
has the smallest variance. Under those five assumptions, nothing else in that
class does better.
:::

## Scope and Limits of the Gauss-Markov Theorem

- It is a claim about a **class**: linear, and unbiased. Step outside either
  and the theorem says nothing.
- It rests on **all five** assumptions, and the fifth in particular.
- It is about **precision**, not about correctness. A biased estimator with a
  tiny variance is outside the class entirely.

::: {.caveat}
Hold on to the fifth assumption. In week 11 the error stops having constant
variance, least squares stops being best, and the standard error you just
learned to read stops being right. That is where robust standard errors come
from, and this theorem is why they are needed.
:::

## Vote: Which Sample Gives a Tighter Estimate?

Two hundred people whose schooling runs from eleven to thirteen years, or
eighty whose schooling runs from nine to twenty.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue, vote again. Then: which of the three ingredients did you trade
against which?
:::

## What Would Have To Be True?

::: {.caveat title="The standing question"}
What would have to be true for this number to mean what we just said it means?
And what is the plausible story where it isn't?
:::

[Candidate this week: unbiasedness is a property of repeated sampling.
It says nothing about the one estimate in front of you, and you will only ever
have one.]

## Application

Simulate. Draw a sample, fit, keep the slope, repeat five hundred times.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote first: if we quadruple the sample size, does the histogram move, narrow,
or both? Take the vote before anything is run.
:::

Lab this week: write the loop yourself, then break one assumption deliberately
and watch which of the two things happens.

<!-- 97-105 min. ConcepTest 4. -->

## Summary of Today's Three Ideas

Today was three separate ideas, each doing one job:

::: {.contributions}
1. **The Gauss-Markov Assumptions.** Each assumption earns one specific result, and none of them is decoration.
2. **Unbiasedness.** Unbiasedness is a statement about where the distribution sits, not about your estimate.
3. **Precision.** Precision comes from sample size, spread in schooling, and a quiet error - and no other linear unbiased estimator beats it.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
Next week: turning one estimate and its standard error into a claim you can defend in writing.
:::

## Derivation: Unbiasedness of Least Squares

Write the estimator as the truth plus a term in the errors, take expectations,
and use the zero conditional mean assumption.

::: {.tablenotes}
Three steps. Substitute the population model into the estimator, split the
result into the truth plus a weighted sum of errors, take the expectation.
The step that does the work is the third, and it works only because of
assumption two. Turn that assumption off and the whole thing fails, which is
exactly what happens in week 8.
:::

[Full derivation. Set as homework; worked solution published with the set.]

## Derivation: The Variance of the Slope

Take the same decomposition and compute its variance instead of its mean.

::: {.tablenotes}
The result has three ingredients, and each one is a panel of the figure you
saw: the error variance on top, the spread of schooling and the sample size
underneath. Reading the formula and reading that figure should feel like the
same activity.
:::

[Full derivation. Set as homework; worked solution published with the set.]
